# Roadmap

This is where SageFs is headed, as far as I can see it. Some of it is being built today and some of it is an idea I haven't worked out yet. I'd rather you see all of it than guess.

## How this page stays true

I don't edit status by hand. Each item can name a landmark, a file and a symbol that will exist in the code once the work does. When it shows up in the tree, the item moves to Built on its own and links to the code. A test fails if this page and the code disagree, so a stale page can't be committed.

Every item that is not built yet links to a plan in [docs/plans](plans/README.md). The plan has the design and the first failing test, and a block at its top that says where the work stands: its status, its branch, the last green commit and the next action. Work can stop and start again with a different person or tool and nobody has to retell it. A test fails if an open item has no plan or a plan has lost its block.

The horizons are guesses about distance and I'm not promising dates. Things move, and the order below is my best current read. If something here matters to you and it's far away, tell me. That moves things more than anything else does.

On the page today: Now 0, Next 6, Later 19, Exploring 20. Already built: 64.

## Next (6)

_Designed, or close to it, and queued behind Now. Weeks to a couple of months._

### Live testing

- [ ] **Debug failing tests properly in VS Code.** Debugging a failing test from the VS Code lens works for one test at a time, and the attach is proven in our own tests, the same case the Neovim item leans on. The daemon now records a debug run's verdict on the test's row, with where its code came from, and no normal run happens in between. It keeps a bounded table of the holds it granted so a verdict lands on the right row, and that table belongs to the daemon since 703a55b1: it was process-wide, and a second daemon in one process could take another's held tests. Several tests go one after another under one attach, driven by the client. Against a real managed debugger (netcoredbg, on 2026-11-10) the hold, the attach, the release and the row all work: the test runs under the debugger, the row shows its verdict with its provenance and no duration, a breakpoint in the test stops the host and the release says so (`host_not_answering`, naming netcoredbg) until the debugger goes on, and a ticket survives a confirming build. That run found two defects, both fixed: the instrumented copy of the assembly named a pdb that did not exist, so no breakpoint in your own test could bind, and a build that confirmed an edit swapped the worker away from a held test. The journeys for all of it are in the `--integration-lt` tier (`debug-row-journeys-run-green`). The extension-host case drives `sagefs.debugTest` in a real VS Code with netcoredbg as the `coreclr` adapter, on a daemon of its own with hot reload off, and it passes: live testing pauses while the test is held, resumes after, and the row carries the debug verdict. Still unproven: Microsoft's own adapter, which is checked by hand per release. Breakpoints in evaluated code wait on `confirm-builds-without-restarting-the-worker`. ([LIVE_TESTING_GUIDE.md](LIVE_TESTING_GUIDE.md), [how-live-testing-works.md](how-live-testing-works.md), [debug-failing-tests-in-vscode.md](plans/debug-failing-tests-in-vscode.md))

### Hot reload

- [ ] **A REPL eval changes the running app.** An eval reaches an app you started from FSI, but not one started with run_app, where only saved files get through. There are two ways in. One writes the evaluated declaration to source and lets save, build and delta carry it, which costs the build. That one is in: an eval that names its file and line writes the declaration back, journaled so it undoes, and it is now driven end to end against a running run_app app in our own tests. The eval writes the declaration back, the file change reaches the worker, and the running app serves the new code. Measured here, the whole route takes about 5.6 seconds, most of it the build. The other grafts FSI's own IL into a delta. In a spike that worked and was served in milliseconds, but the IL lives in the FSI host and the delta chain lives in the worker, and nobody has worked out how it crosses. That one isn't built. ([how-hot-reload-works.md](how-hot-reload-works.md), [repl-eval-reaches-the-running-app.md](plans/repl-eval-reaches-the-running-app.md))

### The REPL

- [ ] **Check the whole project with a file replaced, without building.** FsiMcp has `check_project`: it type-checks a whole project with some files replaced by text you send, without a build and without touching the REPL session, so an agent can ask "does this still compile" before it lands an edit. SageFs has `check_fsharp_code` for a snippet and a build for the project, which costs minutes on a loaded machine. The check itself is written, minus the tool: a pure core (`ProjectCheckCore.fs`) with its tests and a simulation, and an effect module (`CheckProject.fs`) that gets the compiler arguments from a child `dotnet msbuild` run, keeps them until the project file, `Directory.Build.props`, `Directory.Build.targets` or `Directory.Packages.props` changes, builds a stale referenced project once, stops when the client cancels, and returns diagnostics with path, line, column, severity, code and message. Overlays are written as stable files under the temp folder and the compiler is given those paths. The tool registration is a patch file in `docs/plans` that waits for the tool-list work, and nothing has run the design-time MSBuild path against `SageFs.Tests.fsproj` on a quiet machine, so the cost per check is not measured. ([mcp-tools.md](mcp-tools.md), [project-check-with-overlays.md](plans/project-check-with-overlays.md))
- [ ] **One rule decides what a worker's report writes into the registry.** Reading a session's status writes to the registry. `get_session_status` takes the worker's report and, when it differs, stores it so `list_sessions` agrees. The 5 second health probe writes too, by a different rule. The read's rule can store a transient: while a level or a reset replaced the FSI host in place, a read left Starting in the registry for a worker that was Ready, and the level reported Leveled while the daemon held the old host's tests. The probe now retires that within 5 seconds and the symptom is fixed, but the second rule is still there. I would have both ask one pure function, so a read only moves the registry toward settled. The other answers are a read-only read, with `list_sessions` up to 5 seconds behind, or leaving it. It is your decision. ([decisions.md](decisions.md), [session-status-reads-write-the-registry.md](plans/session-status-reads-write-the-registry.md))

### Dashboard

- [ ] **A live bindings view you can switch and keep.** The Live Bindings pane used to draw a badge, a type, a wide pin and the same sentence on every row, so at the default dock two of ten bindings showed, and it looked the same in every workflow. It is one configurable watch view now: one line a row, presets, a recommended preset for each workflow, and a choice kept for each app and workflow through the settings layers. A row says its relation to its source in one word (`tweaked`, `evolved`), and the Changes strip says what Save writes: "Save 9.5 to Tuning.fs:3" for a tweak, Reset, or "Use 1 as the initial value" with its question for a value the program changed. The tabs All, Pinned, Changes and Watch each keep their own view, and Watch holds expressions you add: a name or a field reads from the session's values and runs nothing, and an expression that runs code waits for its Run button. A whole number can be shown as Hex, Binary or a colour, the bar has a chip that says whether the values are `current` or `updating` as the test loop runs, and every one of these is proven in a real browser. Still to build: following a call into the function that builds a value, which is a pure resolver and a test that do not exist yet, spies that re-evaluate a pinned expression each time the loop settles, and the chip's buffer-ahead form. ([live-bindings-watch-view.md](plans/live-bindings-watch-view.md), [more-settings-editable.md](plans/more-settings-editable.md))

### Docs and onboarding

- [ ] **A head-to-head benchmark for REPL servers.** I want to be able to say where SageFs is ahead of another REPL server and where it is behind, with numbers I can defend. The harness drives each server over stdio on the same small project: time to ready, first and follow-up eval, rebuild and continue, a hang, a stack overflow, a failed build, tool-list tokens, and steps from nothing to a first eval. It runs only on a quiet machine, refuses to record a number without the machine, load and versions, and publishes a dated page that credits each tool's author and links each loss to its plan. FsiMcp is the first comparison. Running someone else's package needs my go and a sandbox, so the plan says how, and no timing is written until then. ([repl-loop-benchmarks.md](repl-loop-benchmarks.md), [repl-benchmark-against-other-tools.md](plans/repl-benchmark-against-other-tools.md))

- [ ] **run_tests reuses proven results.** The content-addressed cache that stops a landing being proven twice works only for the cohort landing gate. I'd feed it into run_tests receipts too, and run tests inside the live session once I know a redefinition changes what your compiled tests call. ### Hot reload

- [ ] **Type changes keep your running state.** A record that gains a field can keep its live value today, but only if your app registers a boundary and only for simple fields such as int and string. I want that to need nothing from you and to cover more field kinds, because a type change is the biggest restart left. ([granular-restart-scope.md](granular-restart-scope.md), [decisions.md](decisions.md), [type-change-keeps-state.md](plans/type-change-keeps-state.md))
- [ ] **Adding a field without a restart.** A run_app save that adds a field to a type, or adds a lambda that captures something, still restarts the app. The runtime can take those as deltas. My emitter writes rows only for method bodies and added methods so far. ([how-hot-reload-works.md](how-hot-reload-works.md), [decisions.md](decisions.md), [delta-adds-fields-and-types.md](plans/delta-adds-fields-and-types.md))
- [ ] **Refresh CSS and static files too.** Browser refresh covers your pages when a save lands. CSS, static assets and Razor or Blazor views aren't part of it, and .NET Hot Reload covers them. ([how-hot-reload-works.md](how-hot-reload-works.md), [browser-refresh-beyond-pages.md](plans/browser-refresh-beyond-pages.md))

### The REPL

- [ ] **A profile tool: where the time and allocations went.** FsiMcp has a `profile` tool that runs your F# like an eval and reports where CPU time or allocations went, recorded over EventPipe from outside the process that runs your code. SageFs now has both halves: `profile` runs your code like `send_fsharp_code` while the daemon records the session's FSI host with an installed `dotnet-trace`. With `mode=cpu` it answers with methods by self time and your own code by total time; with `mode=alloc`, with the bytes the runtime sampled by type and by type at the nearest frame of yours. Each row has its share, and the reply says what was not counted. The host loads nothing for it, no package was added (the allocation events are read by a reader of our own), the trace files are removed when the call returns, and a missing tool, a failed attach or a host that ends mid-recording is a named reply that says what to do next. It is classed as an eval tool, so a role without eval never sees it, and it works on Linux and macOS. Both were checked by hand against a real host; the integration-tier cases that hold them to it have not yet run on the machine that ships, a Windows daemon refuses for now, and the CPU table's label for time spent waiting for a garbage collection counts only the one runtime poll a real trace showed. ([profile-tool.md](plans/profile-tool.md))
- [ ] **Sessions learn the right load order.** I stopped this one. I measured four projects, 1,454 source files in all, looking for a project whose opens need a second pass, and found none. The one retry that fires, in SageFs.Simulation, comes from two names discovery can never resolve, which a learned order cannot fix. Nothing needs the learned order today, so I did not merge the code. It is kept on the branch `archive/2026-11-07/rescue-load-order` in case a project ever does. ([sessions-learn-the-load-order.md](plans/sessions-learn-the-load-order.md))
- [ ] **A Jupyter kernel that installs and works.** `sagefs --jupyter` is marked experimental because nothing in my suite opens a ZMQ socket against it. I'd add a one-command install and a test that drives it end to end, then richer output than plain text. ([coming-from-jupyter.md](coming-from-jupyter.md), [Readme.md](../Readme.md), [jupyter-kernel-that-works.md](plans/jupyter-kernel-that-works.md))

### Agents and cohorts

- [ ] **Watch your agents from your phone.** A second listener on your Tailscale address would serve the dashboard read-only to a phone with a short-lived token. A conductor could then approve or veto a landing from a link, but only once the minted handles above exist. ([watch-your-agents-from-your-phone.md](plans/watch-your-agents-from-your-phone.md))

Three pieces of that are in. ### Platform and install

- [ ] **Hot reload checked on Windows and macOS.** My CI is Linux only, so the hot reload detour has no passing evidence on Windows, macOS or arm64, and the docs say so. The one data point so far is bad: on an Apple Silicon Mac the five real-detour tests for generic functions fail, and I don't know why (issue #149). Until someone with a Mac captures the failures, hot reload on macOS is unproven. ([how-hot-reload-works.md](how-hot-reload-works.md), [Readme.md](../Readme.md), [hot-reload-on-windows-and-macos.md](plans/hot-reload-on-windows-and-macos.md))
- [ ] **Start on login for Windows.** Linux gets a systemd user unit and macOS a launchd agent, and each starts the daemon for you. Nothing starts it at login on Windows yet. ([progress.md](progress.md), [Readme.md](../Readme.md), [start-on-login-windows.md](plans/start-on-login-windows.md))
- [ ] **A .NET Framework host for Framework projects.** SageFs refuses a project whose only target is .NET Framework, because its FSI host is a modern .NET process that cannot load Framework assemblies. The host is already built by the project's own SDK behind a process boundary, so a Framework variant is another build of an existing artifact. It would run on Windows only. I want the session to run on the Framework CLR, since driving fsianycpu.exe gives a bare REPL with no hot reload, live testing or coverage. Requested in issue #135. ([ecosystem-compatibility.md](ecosystem-compatibility.md), [how-isolation-works.md](how-isolation-works.md), [dotnet-framework-host.md](plans/dotnet-framework-host.md))
- [ ] **The getter sandbox beyond Linux x86-64.** Clicking a getter in the live-bindings pane runs it under a syscall filter that stops network use and file writes, on Linux x86-64 only. Elsewhere the getter runs under its deadline alone, and the pane says so. ([decisions.md](decisions.md), [getter-sandbox-beyond-linux.md](plans/getter-sandbox-beyond-linux.md))
- [ ] **A token for every daemon call.** The daemon binds loopback only and checks Origin so a web page can't drive it, but nothing authenticates a local caller. A minted token the daemon requires would, and it's the same handle agents need for their own identity. ([mcp-tools.md](mcp-tools.md), [a-token-for-every-daemon-call.md](plans/a-token-for-every-daemon-call.md))
- [ ] **Admit heavy work by measured cost.** Heavy work already takes a lease, and the daemon sheds under memory pressure with a retry hint. It doesn't yet know what a rebuild of your project usually costs, so it reacts instead of predicting. I'd record peak memory and duration per kind of work and admit against the headroom. ([admit-heavy-work-by-measured-cost.md](plans/admit-heavy-work-by-measured-cost.md))

## Exploring (20)

_An idea I'm turning over. No promise, and some of these will die._

### Live testing

- [ ] **Mutation testing in the live session.** Hot-patching a mutant into the running image might cost milliseconds where Stryker.NET pays a build each. Nobody has timed it, and a day against Stryker on a fixture would tell me. ([mutants-in-the-live-session.md](plans/mutants-in-the-live-session.md))
- [ ] **Test selection that learns from history.** Small local models trained on your own run history could rank which tests to run first and flag the flaky ones. It's a parked design with no code, and selection by coverage works without it. ([test-selection-that-learns.md](plans/test-selection-that-learns.md))

### Hot reload

- [ ] **Use the F# compiler's own deltas.** dotnet/fsharp#19941 would have the compiler write metadata deltas itself. If it ships in an SDK, what I wrote becomes the part that applies and confirms them, and it could reach the REPL host too. I'm tracking it and not waiting for it. ([how-hot-reload-works.md](how-hot-reload-works.md), [decisions.md](decisions.md), [use-the-fsharp-compilers-deltas.md](plans/use-the-fsharp-compilers-deltas.md))
- [ ] **Breakpoints in patched code.** Saves land while a debugger is attached, and I've tested that with netcoredbg on four shapes. Nothing sets a breakpoint, steps, or edits a method the debugger is stopped in, because a detour rewrites the first bytes a breakpoint may sit in. ([hot-reload.md](hot-reload.md), [decisions.md](decisions.md), [breakpoints-in-patched-code.md](plans/breakpoints-in-patched-code.md))
- [ ] **Redefine a value a handler renders.** Edit a value that a page handler hands on and the next save is a restart, because I can't tell whether the response kept it. Following the value past the handler would let those patch, and I'd rather prove that than assume it. ([hot-reload.md](hot-reload.md), [redefine-a-value-a-handler-renders.md](plans/redefine-a-value-a-handler-renders.md))
- [ ] **Hot reload without turning tiering off.** Hot reload sessions run with tiered compilation off so a watch on a value can't silently lapse, and that costs warmup time. A cheaper way to keep the watch reliable would let me leave JIT tiering alone. ([hot-reload.md](hot-reload.md), [hot-reload-without-tiering-off.md](plans/hot-reload-without-tiering-off.md))

### The REPL

- [ ] **A notebook that is a window onto a live session.** Cells that update when you edit source, and a value tree as the default output, over the same session your editor and your agent already share. ([coming-from-jupyter.md](coming-from-jupyter.md), [a-notebook-over-a-live-session.md](plans/a-notebook-over-a-live-session.md))
- [ ] **Faster time to Ready.** Warmup is long enough to notice on a bigger solution. Opening namespaces is 60 to 90 percent of it and the replay cache doesn't touch that part, so a precompiled warmup assembly might, once I've measured whether it would help. ([faster-time-to-ready.md](plans/faster-time-to-ready.md))

### Agents and cohorts

- [ ] **A token per sub-agent in Claude Code.** A header is per connection, so sub-agents that share one connection share a token. Only a per-call `_meta` tells them apart, and Claude Code gives the model no per-call header, so a harness hook that sets it would be the way in. ([a-token-per-subagent-in-claude-code.md](plans/a-token-per-subagent-in-claude-code.md))
- [ ] **Claim an interface, not just a file.** An agent would claim a .fsi signature file, every member's session would check its code against it, and a change to it would need a recorded decision. Claims cover only files and projects today. ([claim-an-interface.md](plans/claim-an-interface.md))
- [ ] **Plan a cohort as F# code.** A plan builder would fail at construction if two members claim the same file, and later could propose a claim split from coverage data for you to edit. ([plan-a-cohort-as-code.md](plans/plan-a-cohort-as-code.md))
- [ ] **Fork a cohort or a session at a point.** Replay a session's cells up to one point into a new worktree, or fork a whole cohort at a ledger sequence number, the way git branches a commit. A cell with side effects replays differently, and the result would say so. ([fork-and-rewind.md](plans/fork-and-rewind.md))
- [ ] **A cohort across machines.** Once members are handles instead of sockets, one could join from another machine. The coordination core is already pure and message-passing, so it could cross a network. ([a-cohort-across-machines.md](plans/a-cohort-across-machines.md))
- [ ] **Ask the live codebase in F#.** A type provider over the repo and the cohort would make a misspelled symbol or test name a compile error at the agent's prompt, and active patterns could filter the cohort in code. This is research. ([ask-the-live-codebase-in-fsharp.md](plans/ask-the-live-codebase-in-fsharp.md))
- [ ] **A REPL guard for agents other than Claude.** The hook that sends an agent back to the REPL instead of running dotnet build is a Claude Code hook. Other agent tools have nothing like it yet. ([agents.md](agents.md), [repl-guard-for-other-agents.md](plans/repl-guard-for-other-agents.md))
- [ ] **Check the scope before the write, not after.** A claim is policy today: it refuses another member's claim over the same file, but nothing stops a process writing outside the checkout, and the daemon says that about itself. The one component sitting between an agent and its own file tools could ask where a write is going before it happens, which is the difference between a claim and a boundary. ([agents.md](agents.md), [check-the-scope-before-the-write.md](plans/check-the-scope-before-the-write.md))
- [ ] **Drive real coding agents as cohort members.** One process would hold the seat, mint a token per run and drive Claude, Copilot, OpenCode or Pi over the Agent Client Protocol as a member with its own claims and landings, answering that member's permission requests from the scope it holds. It has to join the cohort before it mints anything, because a fresh connection is Anonymous and the very first mint would be refused. ([agents.md](agents.md), [drive-real-agents-as-members.md](plans/drive-real-agents-as-members.md))
- [ ] **Confirmation gates in every agent host.** Where a host can prompt before a tool call, a small plugin could ask there, which covers the clients a server-side prompt can never reach. Since 2026-11-07 the server asks about one tool only, `manage_local_data`, because stopping and resetting sessions are normal steps of the loop and no longer prompt anywhere. That shrank this item to one tool, so the plan needs re-scoping before anyone builds it. None of the hosts has been run yet. ([agents.md](agents.md), [confirmation-gates-in-every-agent-host.md](plans/confirmation-gates-in-every-agent-host.md))

### Editors

- [ ] **Rider, Zed, Helix and Emacs.** SageFs speaks HTTP and SSE, so any editor could connect, but only VS Code and Neovim have clients. When people ask for more, Rider comes up most. ([agents.md](agents.md), [editors-beyond-vscode-and-neovim.md](plans/editors-beyond-vscode-and-neovim.md))

## Built (64)

_These were on this page and are in the code now. Whether a build has shipped is in [the release notes](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/releases) and [what SageFs has become](progress.md)._

### Live testing

- [x] **A test receipt says what source it ran on.** If you edit a test file and don't rebuild, `run_tests` used to say "3 passed" with no warning. Now every receipt carries whether the source is in sync, stale (naming the files), being rebuilt, or unknown and why. A pass over stale source reads "passed, but on STALE source" and is never plain AllPassed. It's also on `get_session_status` and `list_sessions`, next to the REPL-behind state. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/SourceState.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/SourceState.fs)
- [x] **A pending test is skipped, not passed.** An Expecto `ptest` used to run its body and count as passed. It's now reported as skipped and never run, and a run with one is Incomplete, not AllPassed. If anything is focused with `ftest`, the unfocused tests are reported as skipped too, matching what Expecto itself does. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/LiveTestingExecutors.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/LiveTestingExecutors.fs)
- [x] **Edits during a worker swap are judged.** An edit typed while the confirming build replaces the worker used to be lost. A type-check or an eval now waits for a Ready worker and believes an answer only from the worker it asked. Code: [`SageFs/LiveCheckRelay.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/LiveCheckRelay.fs)
- [x] **Confirm builds without restarting the worker.** The confirming build used to replace your worker, so a value you had bound in the REPL, a script you had loaded and the unsaved buffers of other files went with it. Now a session that holds any of that is confirmed in a throwaway worker, started on the build and stopped afterwards, and its own worker is never touched. If there is no room for a second worker, or the session's startup starts an app on a fixed port, the rows say `NotConfirmed` and why, and nothing is touched. A session that holds nothing is swapped as before, which keeps its coverage current. A throwaway worker's coverage is not applied yet, so a session that holds something keeps the coverage of its own worker until that worker is swapped. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ConfirmationVenue.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ConfirmationVenue.fs)
- [x] **Bound what a connection is sent on connect.** A connection is sent the list of files that have annotations in one frame, and an editor asks for the ones it has open. Before, a connect sent the annotations and coverage badges of every file, one frame each, and on a project of 1,629 files that had sent 2.7 MB after 100 seconds without finishing. Now a connect to a session on SageFs.Tests, with 17,973 tests discovered, is 14 frames and 116 KB. While a suite runs, only the files whose annotations changed are pushed. Code: [`SageFs.Core/SseWriter.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/SseWriter.fs)
- [x] **No live request dropped during a swap.** A check that waited out the 30 second swap bound was dropped instead of retried, and running affected tests or discovery dropped a request that found no worker. The gate now parks on the manager's own AwaitReady for the bound a rebuild's own wait uses, then judges the state that wait released, so a code tool waits for the replacement instead of being refused the moment a swap begins. Code: [`SageFs/Mcp.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/Mcp.fs)
- [x] **The debug-row journeys run green, then go back in the tier.** Two journeys check that after a test is debugged, its row shows the verdict the debugger gave it, with where its code came from and no duration, which a normal run's verdict has. One is a single test and one is three tests under one attach. They are in the `--integration-lt` tier and they run green against a real managed debugger, netcoredbg 3.2.0-1092, driven through its console (`--interpreter=cli --attach <pid>`, then `continue`, then the release). The earlier plan failed because the only debugger on the machine, `dotnet-debug`, is an inspector with no `continue` that never makes the host see a debugger. The tier also holds a case where a test held at a breakpoint stops the host and the release says `host_not_answering` and names netcoredbg, with the ticket still good once the debugger goes on, and two cases where a ticket held across a confirming build is not lost. The hand run found two defects, both fixed: the instrumented copy of the assembly named a pdb that did not exist, so a breakpoint in your own test could not bind, and a confirming build swapped the worker away from a held test when the session held nothing else. The gate sets `SAGEFS_REQUIRE_DEBUGGER=1`, so a machine without netcoredbg fails these cases with the install command. The hosted pull-request job has no netcoredbg and says SKIPPED. The extension-host debug case in `--integration-host` has a daemon of its own with hot reload off and passes. Code: [`SageFs.Tests/LiveTestingShards.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Tests/LiveTestingShards.fs)

### Hot reload

- [x] **The REPL says when it is behind.** After a save is patched into your running app, the REPL and the live tests still run the build from before it. Nothing used to say so. Now the session carries a named state, and `get_session_status`, `list_sessions`, `send_fsharp_code`, `run_tests` and the dashboard card all say the REPL is behind, which declarations changed, and what bringing it level costs. Code: [`SageFs.Core/SessionManager.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/SessionManager.fs)
- [x] **Saves to run_app apps patch in place.** A save to an app you started with run_app is handed to the runtime as a metadata delta, so the process keeps its state. On the test fixture a save was served in 1.8 to 2.6 seconds against 6 to 8.5 for the restart it replaced, and `SAGEFS_METADATA_DELTA=off` puts the old behavior back. Code: [`SageFs.Host/RunAppDelta.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Host/RunAppDelta.fs)
- [x] **Generic functions patch in every instantiation.** A save to a generic function reaches every instantiation the runtime compiled, including a float or struct first used after the save. If your code calls MakeGenericMethod anywhere, a save to a generic function still restarts and names why. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Middleware/HotReloadCore.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Middleware/HotReloadCore.fs)
- [x] **Hot reload save times are measured.** A test tier times saves against a real running app and fails if the p95 drifts. It's one machine and one small app, and I have no Microsoft figure to set it against. Code: [`SageFs.Tests/HotReloadLatency.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Tests/HotReloadLatency.fs)
- [x] **Level the REPL after a patch without losing it.** After a save is patched into your running app, the REPL's FSI host is older than the app, and the only fix was a rebuild reset that stopped the app. Now the session brings the host level by itself when that loses nothing. It asks the worker for a fresh host, which takes about 2 seconds and keeps the app's process and state, and then fetches the tests and coverage maps again. A level waits for a test run in flight, and a run that arrives during a level waits for the level. It leaves a REPL alone that holds something of yours: an eval it ran since the host started, a value from your init script, or tests an editor buffer defined. The session's state says what held it, in `blockedBy`. A host whose last reset took longer than 10 seconds is left to you too, because SageFs.Tests took 25 to 39 seconds under load where a small project takes 2.6 to 3.4, and the session that verifies cohort landings is never leveled. This release also fixed two ways the state could say Leveled while the daemon held the old host's tests: a status read could leave Starting in the registry for a worker that was Ready, and a level's refetched tests were dropped while it did. I measured the 10 second budget on a loaded machine and have not repeated it on an idle one. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ReplLeveling.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ReplLeveling.fs)
- [x] **Nudge a value in the running app.** The `nudge_value` tool lists the literals and expressions in a file the session owns, writes one of them back as just that range, journals the write before it lands, and undoes it exactly. A stale address is refused with what moved, and a write that does not type-check shows up in the reload verdict and rolls back. Agents and scripts can use it today. Code: [`SageFs/McpNudge.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/McpNudge.fs)
- [x] **A knob for the value you are nudging.** The dashboard's Live Bindings pane has a knob on every value a project file holds. A row says where its value lives (`in source`, `not in a file`, `ambiguous` when two files declare the name, and the reasons a write cannot be offered), and the control follows what the file actually spells: a real gets a drag handle, step buttons and the arrow keys, a bool a switch, a string or a character a field, a formula (`gravity * 2.0`) an expression field, and a value made of parts becomes rows of its own. The step count is turned into the literal by the daemon, so `1.0` stays `1.0`, `0x1F` stays hex and units stay. Every write goes through the same nudge door the tool uses, with the hash the row last showed, its own undo and redo, and a refusal that says the rule and what to do. What it does not do yet: apply a value to the running app before you save it, and say when the app copied a value at startup. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/Tweak/BindingTweak.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/Tweak/BindingTweak.fs)
- [x] **A knob in the editors too.** The dashboard has the knob, and now both editors do too. Neovim scrubs with Alt-k and Alt-j: each press runs the same inspect-locate-bump-set flow `:SageFsNudge` runs, so the rules and the undo are the daemon's, and a count multiplies the steps. VS Code scrubs by dragging across a number with the multi-cursor modifier held, because its API never reports that a modifier is down; what it reports is the second cursor an Alt+click adds. Both write through `nudge_value`, so the journal, the seen hash, the refusal and the type-check rollback all apply. Code: [`sagefs-vscode/src/NudgeKnob.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/sagefs-vscode/src/NudgeKnob.fs)
- [x] **Callers in other files follow a signature change.** When a save re-signs or removes a function, the reload report now lists every caller in another file that still calls the old one, with file, line and the next action, and it clears when that file is saved and patched. A caller saved on its own lands against the new definition. If the other files can't be searched it says so instead of staying quiet. A caller that needs no edit stays listed until a restart. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/CallerState.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/CallerState.fs)

### The REPL

- [x] **A rebuild is waited on, not skipped.** `get_session_status` with `wait_seconds` now waits for a rebuild in progress and answers when the new worker is ready, or Faulted with the build's own error. It used to answer "not needed" while the rebuild was still running, so a caller had to poll. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ReadyWait.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ReadyWait.fs)
- [x] **Eval output shaped for the agent that reads it.** A result over 4,000 characters keeps its first two thirds and its last third with a line between that says how many characters were cut, and the whole value is still bound as `it`. Both kinds of session print under one set of limits (20 items, depth 6, width 78, size 600), which cut the echo of a `let` of 24 nested records from 4,521 characters to 781. Output a background thread writes between calls was dropped before; it now leads the next successful reply under a label, and a test drives the real `sagefs mcp` bridge with a thread running in the user's code to prove it. Echoing only the type of a `let` is built and off, because the editors show the value. The limits are not yet a field you can set per directory, and the skill's loop doc does not yet describe a clipped reply. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/EvalResultSummary.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/EvalResultSummary.fs)
- [x] **A hung or runaway eval answers in bounded time.** An eval that loops, waits or recurses used to leave the caller waiting for the worker's ten minutes, and cancelling it ended the call while the host kept running the code, so the next eval queued behind a run nobody waited for. Now `send_fsharp_code` takes `timeout_seconds` (default 120), cancels at the limit and says so, and a host that does not stop within ten seconds of a cancel is killed with a message that says what was lost. A stack overflow reports `stack overflow` with the recursing function, and every eval runs on a 256 MB stack like FsiMcp's. Code: [`SageFs.Core/EvalBound.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/EvalBound.fs)
- [x] **A cost line on a slow or allocation-heavy eval.** An eval that took half a second or allocated 100 MB ends its reply, failed or not, with one line of time, bytes allocated and GC counts, in the shape FsiMcp prints. The isolated host reads the counters around each eval and returns them as a typed field of the protocol; the daemon writes the line, so a light eval costs no extra tokens. Bytes are the whole process's, because the eval thread's own counter read 2 KB for 100 MB allocated by four tasks. The session's timeline keeps each eval's cost now, and `get_eval_timeline` shows the bytes beside the duration. Still open: the dashboard's push reads a separate store that takes no cost (`McpContext.RecordEval` still takes three arguments), the timeline records a failed eval as Succeeded, and the thresholds were picked before a daemon had a day of history to check them against. Code: [`SageFs/EvalReply.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/EvalReply.fs)
- [x] **Session options you can set.** FsiMcp lets you set Server GC, an artifacts path that keeps build output out of the project, environment variables for the session process, and a prelude. SageFs already has the prelude, as `.SageFs/init.fsx`. A directory's `config.fsx` takes the other three now: `Gc = ServerGc`, `SessionEnv` and `Artifacts = ArtifactsIn <absolute path>`, one named field each with a closed type, a poisoned variable refused with its reason, and a relative artifacts path refused rather than guessed against a directory. The daemon reads the config once, when a session is created, and the worker gets the whole options value in one variable, so the worker no longer evaluates `config.fsx`, and that took one FSI host start out of every session. The artifacts path moves the session's own builds and its project load, proved by a real build and a real load. `config.fsx` also accepted `InitScript`, `IsRoot` and `SessionName` and nothing read them, so those three are gone, and `DefaultArgs` reaches the FSI host. The three options also have rows in the Settings page's Session group (`session.gc`, `session.environment`, `session.artifactsPath`), saved per directory and applied to the next session started there, and a field in `config.fsx` wins over its row. A refused value shows its reason and next step where it was typed. Each session now fixes its own options when its worker first starts, so creating another session in the same directory cannot change a running one's restarts or rebuilds. A project that sets `ArtifactsPath` in its own build files keeps it: I tested the mix, found that the build wrote to the project's folder while the project load looked in the session's, and now the session's request is refused with a message naming both folders. The outcome gates start real sessions and read the effect back from inside them: `GCSettings.IsServerGC`, an environment value, and the build output under the artifacts path. Still open: the conflict check asks MSBuild about the first project of a session only, a session's own status does not list its options, and the gates have run on one machine. Code: [`SageFs.Core/SessionOptionSettings.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/SessionOptionSettings.fs)

### Isolation

- [x] **A session builds against the Core its project brings.** A session on a project in a repo that builds its own SageFs.Core now compiles against that Core, not the daemon's older one. Before, building SageFs.Tests in a worktree failed against the old Core and printed a wrong compile-order hint. A project that can't be read is refused with the path and the reason. The daemon and its FSI host still match Cores by version number, so a worktree Core and an older daemon can disagree at load time until they're built together. Code: [`SageFs.Core/CoreEvidence.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/CoreEvidence.fs)
- [x] **Native NuGet packages load in sessions.** Someone reported a `#r` NuGet package with a native library failing in plain FSI. I couldn't reproduce that on Linux: SQLite, SkiaSharp and LibGit2Sharp all load in plain FSI and in a bare SageFs session. What did fail was a project session, because the package's native library sits in the NuGet cache and the isolated host never looked there. The host now finds it from the project's restore, and a library that won't load is named with its package, this runtime and what to do. Windows, macOS and arm64 are untested. Code: [`SageFs.Core/NativeResolution.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/NativeResolution.fs)
- [x] **A sandboxed getter leaves no filtered thread behind.** When the live bindings pane runs a property getter on a click, the getter goes on a fresh thread under a seccomp filter that stops network, writes and new processes. A pool worker made on its behalf used to be born under that filter and keep it for the life of the process, so the host's own writes failed on it afterwards: 768 of 768 pool file writes on .NET 10, five threads left filtered on .NET 11. The filter now refuses thread creation, the pool is made ready on the caller's thread before the call, and the pool's limits are held while it runs, because refusing alone corrupts the pool's accounting and hangs the next `Task.Run`. After a call the kernel names no filtered thread, and a getter that tries to start one gets an exception inside the getter. Still open: the runtime's tiering thread is refused too and nothing here covers it, one `InvalidCastException` out of a getter was seen once and has not come back, and the hold's timeout is proven in a child process and not in a long-running host. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ThreadSandbox.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ThreadSandbox.fs)

### Agents and cohorts

- [x] **An agent's landed work reaches your running app.** When agents land work in the shared trunk, the app running in the trunk session picks it up live with its state kept. `get_cohort_status` and the dashboard show each landing's result per file, including the mechanism, and a landing that needs a restart says why. A landing that fails verification never reaches the app. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/TrunkFollow.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/TrunkFollow.fs)
- [x] **The daemon stops a session an agent forgot.** An agent makes a session, wanders off, and the worker sits there for days. Now the daemon stops it once the connection that made it has been gone and the session has been idle for 12 hours, and says why. A session you made from the dashboard, the CLI or an editor is never stopped this way. `SAGEFS_ABANDONED_SESSION_HOURS` sets the time, and 0 turns it off. Code: [`SageFs.Core/SessionReaper.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/SessionReaper.fs)
- [x] **Keep a cohort run and play it back.** `sagefs cohort-export` writes a cohort's ledger from the local database to a file, with no daemon running, and `sagefs play` reads that file back. A finished cohort's rows get pruned after a while, so the export is the only way to keep a run. A file that mixes cohorts from different repositories is refused, with the scopes listed. Code: [`SageFs/CohortExportCommand.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/CohortExportCommand.fs)
- [x] **Each agent counts as its own member.** Sub-agents of one Claude Code session share one MCP connection, so SageFs saw them as a single member and the build and test leases collided. The conductor now mints a token per run with `mint_member`, each token is its own member with its own claims and leases, and a token outranks the connection it arrives on. A platform sets it in a header or in MCP `_meta`, never as a tool argument. Tokens live in memory, so a daemon restart means minting new ones. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Capability.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Capability.fs)
- [x] **A member's role says which tools it can call.** An Observer used to be able to call send_fsharp_code, because authority only gated the cohort's own tools. A member token now has one of four roles (Observer, Analysis, Verifier, Implementer), each a set of tool classes, and a call outside the role is refused with the role, the tool and what to do. `tools/list` shows a token only what it can call, and `SAGEFS_IDENTITY_POLICY=TokenRequired` makes a connection with no token read-only. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Capability.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Capability.fs)
- [x] **A member's id is no longer the bearer handle.** A member's id in `get_cohort_status`, the cohort frame and the ledger was the MCP session id, which is the credential a request is bound to, so anyone who read the status could act as the conductor. The id is a fingerprint of it now, and a test fails if any cohort output carries a handle. Code: [`SageFs.Core/MemberTable.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/MemberTable.fs)
- [x] **A stdio bridge stays the same cohort member across a daemon restart.** After a daemon upgrade the stdio bridge re-initialized with a new MCP session, and a member's id was a fingerprint of the session id, so the conductor came back as a stranger while its old self held the seat for up to 30 minutes. The bridge now makes a random key when it starts and sends it on every request, the daemon names the member after a fingerprint of that key, and the same client is the same member through a restart or a reconnect. The reaper also counts an open push stream and any admitted call as presence, where it used to count only an eval, so a conductor that waits on its agents keeps its seat. Code: [`SageFs.Core/MemberTable.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/MemberTable.fs)
- [x] **A claim path means one thing.** `src/Foo/../Bar/x.fs` did not overlap `src/Bar/x.fs`, so two members could hold the same file and a prefix check could be walked around. Claim paths are canonical at the boundary now, and a path that leaves the repo is refused. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Cohort.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Cohort.fs)
- [x] **Veto and delegate in a cohort.** The conductor can hand the seat to a present member with `delegate_conductor`. A seated Implementer, Verifier or the conductor can `veto_landing` with a reason, the conductor clears it with `resolve_veto`, and a landing's own requester can `withdraw_landing`. A veto on a landing that already landed is refused, not ignored, and `get_cohort_status` and the dashboard panel show who vetoed and why. A vacant seat still can't be filled from the tool surface. Code: [`SageFs/McpCohortTools.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/McpCohortTools.fs)
- [x] **A person can seat a conductor.** When a cohort's conductor leaves or goes silent the seat stays empty, and no tool could fill it, so a cohort whose conductor left could only be reset by wiping its ledger. `sagefs cohort seat <member id>` fills it: the person who runs the daemon names a present member, the operator credential is checked, and the ledger records `ConductorSeated` with the vacancy it ended. A held seat, an absent member and a member under a token are refused with the reason, and no member token reaches the route. The credential is a file the operating-system user can read, so a process running as that user can run the command; no MCP tool can seat anyone without the person's yes (`seat_conductor`). With no member id the command lists who is present and where the seat stands. Code: [`SageFs/CohortSeatCommand.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/CohortSeatCommand.fs)
- [x] **A seated member can ask for a conductor, and a person answers.** The person who had to leave their conversation to type `sagefs cohort seat` can now be asked in it. `seat_conductor` is a tool a seated Implementer calls; the daemon asks the person at the client through MCP elicitation, naming the repository, who would sit, who held the seat and why it is empty, and seats nobody without a ticked box. A decline, a dismissal, silence, a failed question, an accept with nothing ticked and a client that offers no elicitation all refuse and change nothing, and the refusal names the command and the dashboard's new Seat button, which asks first and needs the one-use ticket its page was rendered with. The command is built from a `SeatApproval` that only the accepted question can make, so no MCP tool seats anyone without it, and a member under a token neither asks nor is seated. The daemon knows the client accepted and cannot know a person did, and the page's ticket does not authenticate a person: a process that can load the page can read it. Code: [`SageFs.Core/SeatingFlow.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/SeatingFlow.fs)
- [x] **A seated member can ask to replace a silent conductor, and a person answers.** A conductor whose connection is gone keeps a bound seat until its lease lapses, and replacing it needed `sagefs cohort seat --replace` from a shell. `seat_conductor` now takes `replaces`, the holder's member id, and the daemon asks the person at the client the same question, naming the holder and how long it has been silent (or that it renewed its lease a few minutes ago). Only an accept with the box ticked replaces it: the command is `ReplaceConductor`, built from a `SeatApproval` that carries the holder the person was shown and that only the accepted question makes, so no agent replaces a conductor on its own say-so. The cohort's compare-and-swap still runs when the command commits, so a seat that changed hands while the person read the question refuses and names the new holder, and the simulation holds that a bound seat changes hands only on a yes and only from the holder shown. A holder that is not the holder, an empty seat, a holder replaced by itself and a member under a token refuse before anybody is asked. The dashboard's cohort panel shows a Replace button for each present member while the holder is silent, which asks first and carries a one-use ticket issued for that pair of holder and member. A headless browser clicked it on the real page markup. Still unproven: the button against a live daemon's page, and how a real client words the question. A holder that is only slow can be replaced if the person says yes. Code: [`SageFs.Core/SeatingFlow.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/SeatingFlow.fs)
- [x] **A person can replace a conductor whose connection is gone.** A conductor whose connection is gone keeps the seat until its lease lapses, 30 minutes, and a seating over a bound seat is refused, so the person at the machine could only wait. `sagefs cohort seat <member id> --replace <holder id>` replaces the holder: it names the holder it replaces and is refused when that is no longer the holder, the target must be present and not under a token, and the replaced holder becomes an ordinary member (presence and claims untouched). The ledger records `ConductorReplaced` with the former holder. Without `--replace` a bound seat is still refused, and the refusal says who holds it, whether it is silent and for how long, when its lease lapses and the exact command; `get_cohort_status` and the dashboard panel say the same for a silent holder. No MCP tool or token can build the command. The dashboard button is P12's `SeatApproval`, which takes the replace mode with the person's yes. Code: [`SageFs/CohortSeatCommand.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/CohortSeatCommand.fs)
- [x] **A member token bound to one session.** A minted token now names the one session or checkout it may route to. A tool that takes a session id or a working directory is held to that on every call, a session list and the session resources are cut to it, and a refusal says which rule it hit and what to do. `mint_member` takes a `session_id`, and its `working_directory` has to be an absolute path. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Capability.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Capability.fs)
- [x] **One typed list of what counts as destructive.** SageFs could say who may call a tool, but nothing said what calling it does to your work. There is now one `Set<ToolName>` on the same DU the authority gate reads, held to the registered tools by a test so a renamed tool cannot leave a stale name behind, and `tools/list` publishes it as MCP's own `destructiveHint`, so a client asks the server instead of keeping a copy of the list itself. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Affordances.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Affordances.fs)
- [x] **A small tool list for a first session.** A client that connected to SageFs was shown 72 tools, 112,840 characters of definitions, about 28,200 tokens by the usual rough count of four characters a token, before its first message. FsiMcp, a seven-tool F# REPL server, lists 5,606 characters. Every tool is now listed with one sentence of at most 160 characters, and its full manual is one call away: `discover_features` with `tool`. A parameter that many tools share, such as `working_directory`, which was described 18 ways, has a few named sentences. The whole list is 38,379 characters for 73 tools, and a ratchet that only goes down holds it there. A daemon started with `SAGEFS_TOOL_LIST=Starter` shows a caller that presents nothing nine tools, 5,521 characters, and every other tool stays callable by name. A member token and the operator credential keep the lists they had. The starter list is opt-in. It becomes the default once a measured pass rate on a fixed task set is no lower than with the full list, and nobody has run that yet. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ToolList.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ToolList.fs)
- [x] **A conductor can clear the claims a lapsed member left behind.** A member that went silent used to keep its `Held` claims, and the scope stayed shut to everyone else until its 30 minute lease lapsed. Now the conductor clears them with `release_claim`. Naming a claim that is not its own is a clear when the holder has had no open stream and no call for two minutes (the measure that already calls a seat's holder silent), and when the claim is orphaned and there is no present member to hand it to. A holder that is here is refused, with how long it has been silent and how long it must be. The fence moves on, so the old holder's late release is refused as stale and a landing it had queued is blocked as stale when it reaches the front. The ledger records `ClaimCleared` with who held it, how long it had been silent and who cleared it, `get_cohort_status` marks each clearable claim on its line, and the Neovim cohort view shows the mark. A call under a member token never clears. I did not put a person's yes on it: the conductor already reassigns claims on its own say-so, and the clear is a release that the fence makes safe. An exhaustive membership model proves a clear is the conductor's, never takes a present holder's claim and moves only that claim, with a twin for each rule; pure cases and one real daemon with three connections cover the orphaned path. Still open: the dashboard's cohort panel has no Clear button and `sagefs cohort` has no clear command (a person replaces a silent conductor first, then the new conductor clears), and the silent-holder path on a real daemon rests on the model and the pure cases, because a test cannot wait two minutes. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Cohort.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Cohort.fs)
- [x] **A big landing waits on the run's progress and not a clock.** The cohort's landing gate used to give up two and a half minutes after it asked, and the executor cancelled the run two minutes after it started, so a run that was still reporting was cut: one cohort run asked for 19067 tests and 18529 never reported. The wait now ends when the count of reported tests stops rising for a stall window (`RunStall`), in the gate and in the worker, and names how many reported and how many did not; a test that never reported still fails the landing. A project file change is read into a closed set of changes: anything but the compile list runs the whole suite, and a compile-list edit selects the tests that cover the files whose meaning it can have changed, read from the file texts, so two test files inserted in the middle of 1096 select two files and not 935. Timed in a session at a load of 45 against a daemon that does not run the fix, 18886 tests were cut at the old cap with 17193 unreported. Still open: no real landing has gone through a daemon running this build, and a whole run through the verifier has not been timed to its end. Code: [`SageFs.Core/Features/RunStall.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/Features/RunStall.fs)
- [x] **Ask you before a tool clears your local data.** The server asks you itself, over MCP's own elicitation request, for exactly one tool: `manage_local_data`, which clears the local stores SageFs keeps on your machine. Those belong to no session and an agent has no reason to clear them mid-task. The call stops after the four gates already there and before its body, names what it is about to take away, and a decline refuses it the way a gate rejection does. The tier sits on the same `ToolName` the authority gate reads rather than in another string list, and it says out loud that a client which never offers elicitation gets no prompt at all, which is the case the stdio bridge re-handshakes into. `stop_session`, `reset_fsi_session`, `hard_reset_fsi_session`, `switch_workflow` and `stop_app` never ask, for any session: an agent calls them as normal steps of its loop, and a prompt on a routine step gets clicked through. They stay marked destructive on `tools/list`, which is information and not a prompt. Code: [`SageFs/McpServer.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/McpServer.fs)
- [x] **Ask what is inside a name, a page at a time.** `list_members` takes a qualified name and answers with its members a page at a time. The reply gives a total that is either exact or marked as a lower bound, a count for each real kind (classes, modules, methods and so on) with the kinds you can step into first, and a footer naming the offset of the next page. A name that lists nothing says why: it is a leaf, an empty container, or it does not resolve under its parent. The kind comes from the compiler through the worker. Before, the daemon guessed it from the shape of the name, and every reply stopped at 50 members whatever the real size. Code: [`SageFs/McpMemberPage.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/McpMemberPage.fs)
- [x] **Walk the rest of the symbol ladder.** The references rung is built: `list_references` takes a qualified name and lists every definition and use the compiler resolves to it across the session's projects, a page at a time. Its first line is the scope (project-wide, partial with the projects it did not reach, or unavailable with the reason), so a count never travels without how far the compiler looked, and one budget covers all the projects together. What remains of the progressive map plan: the name-path fallback for a stale reference, and per-tool result-size ratchet rows so a ladder reply can never become the map again. Code: [`SageFs/McpNamePath.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/McpNamePath.fs)

### Editors

- [x] **Debug a failing test from Neovim.** The daemon side is done: one route holds the test and hands back a process id to attach to, and another releases it. The Neovim side is done too, in the sagefs.nvim repo: `:SageFsDebugTest` puts a failing test on the board and wires nvim-dap to those routes, on `<leader>rtg` and `D` on a panel row. The release goes out on `configurationDone`, when the adapter has really attached, so a slow attach is the daemon's to wait out rather than a grace period on this side. And the attach is now proven in our own tests: a real debugger attaches to the process the daemon names, lists that process's threads, and the held test runs when the debugger lets it go. Code: [`SageFs.Tests/DebugAttachJourneyTests.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Tests/DebugAttachJourneyTests.fs)
- [x] **The Neovim plugin catches up with the daemon.** The plugin shows hot reload's pending and never-entered states, the live-values pane with its Safe mode click, workflow switching and the session's own app state, and it names the session on every session-scoped call. It reads a tool's answer as its first text block, finds a nudged value by the range the daemon reports, sends the session's id with every nudge, shows a vetoed landing with who vetoed it and why, and lists the files a re-sign left on the old method with how sure each match is. The slow-eval heartbeat is wired too: while an eval runs the output section ticks its elapsed time, a beat aimed at another file cannot corrupt it, and the line stops the moment eval_result lands. Code: [`../sagefs.nvim/lua/sagefs/dashboard/state.lua`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/sagefs.nvim/blob/master/lua/sagefs/dashboard/state.lua)

### Dashboard

- [x] **More settings editable from the dashboard.** Every `SAGEFS_*` variable that `Timeouts.fs` and `SageFsConfig.fs` read has a row on the Settings page, and a ratchet at zero fails the suite when a new one is read without a row. A row shows the value in use, the layer it came from (default, global file, repo file, environment variable, flag), what you saved if that differs, and whether the change applies live or after a restart. A variable or flag that overrides a saved value is named on the row: "Saved X. Ignored while NAME is set." A variable that is not for editing, the bind host and the ones SageFs sets itself, has a read-only row that says why. The daemon builds one settings snapshot at start and hands it to each worker and FSI host as an argument, so a saved value reaches them without being copied into the environment. The browser journey ran against the earlier environment import and has not been rerun against the snapshot, and the cells it does not cover are listed in the plan. Code: [`SageFs.Core/EnvBackedRows.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/EnvBackedRows.fs)
- [x] **Dashboard panels that follow your context.** One pure function decides, for every context panel, whether it is shown, hidden with a reason, or quiet because it has nothing to report: hot reload, live testing, cohort, friction, diagnostics, failing tests and alarms. A hidden panel leaves a one-line reason where it would have been, and offers the next step when there is one: live testing off carries a Turn on button, and hot reload names the workflow switcher. A panel with nothing to report draws nothing, diagnostics that were never checked say so instead of reading as clean, and the cohort panel shows while a cohort is running or still holds an orphaned claim or a landing. A browser matrix checks eleven states at 375, 768 and 1400 px. The live bindings becoming a real pane in REPL mode and a pane moving between regions are not built; they belong to the move and dock item. Code: [`SageFs/DashboardPanelContext.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/DashboardPanelContext.fs)
- [x] **App output in its own pane.** stdout and stderr from a running app get their own pane with follow, pause and search, so a chatty app stops burying your evals. The daemon holds one AppOutputPane per session, fed the same lines the transcript is fed from; the dock decides from that buffer and draws the answer, so the two cannot disagree about what the app wrote. Code: [`SageFs/AppOutputView.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/AppOutputView.fs)
- [x] **A guided new-session dialog.** A plus button on the Sessions list opens a dialog that finds projects under a directory you can edit, says in a line what each workflow means, and warns before you make a second session in the same directory, naming the one that exists. A refusal from the daemon shows in the dialog with its next action, and Create closes it into a starting card at once. The no-session picker's Open Directory card still has its own form. Code: [`SageFs/NewSessionDialog.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/NewSessionDialog.fs)
- [x] **A discovery event fits the stream it rides.** A suite of 2,604 tests reached the editor as one SSE event of about 990 KB: the whole discovery list in a single `data:` line, replayed to every connection that catches up on /events. Size was not what broke it. The reader has no size limit and the daemon writes whole frames; what broke it was a buffer that outlived its connection, so a reconnect inherited the dead connection's partial line, and that is fixed and proven, zero parse errors with the reset and one without. What is left is cost: the daemon already fetches discovery over the worker wire, so a summary on the stream with the list behind a fetch takes a catch-up from 990 KB to a few dozen bytes. I would send the summary first and let a client that wants the list ask for it, and whichever shape I pick the editor, the plugin and the dashboard all have to read it. Code: [`SageFs/SseEvent.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/SseEvent.fs)

### Platform and install

- [x] **Slow machines get timeouts that fit them.** On an old quad core with a spinning disk a session never reached Ready, because the 30 second silence limit killed the worker mid-build and the retries repeated the same 30. SageFs now probes the machine, files it as Fast, Standard, Constrained or Minimal, and scales the waits that are for the machine. A start that runs out of patience retries with a longer one, and a give-up names the wait, the attempts and what to set. On that machine it now reaches Ready in about a minute cold and 17 seconds warm. Code: [`SageFs.Core/MachineTier.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/MachineTier.fs)
- [x] **SageFs tidies what agents leave behind.** Agents leave worktrees, branches and gate checkouts behind, and on my machine 65 old gate records alone came to 17.6 GB. A dashboard panel, two MCP tools and `sagefs hygiene` list the leftovers and tidy only the safe ones, after you confirm the exact plan you were shown. Code: [`SageFs.Core/WorkspaceHygiene.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/WorkspaceHygiene.fs)
- [x] **The daemon tidies the workspace by itself.** Workspace hygiene used to tidy only when a person or an agent asked, so on my machine about 25 worktrees and 49 GB piled up over five weeks, some holding commits or uncommitted files that exist nowhere else. The daemon now sweeps at start, every quarter of an hour and when a session stops. It writes each agent worktree into a ledger, commits uncommitted files to a salvage branch without touching the worktree, and, with `hygiene.autoTidy` on, removes only what is provably safe once the ledger has seen it quiet for a day, keeping a restore ref for a commit the base only has by content. Work that exists nowhere else leads the status line, the dashboard card and `sagefs hygiene`, with how old the oldest is, and `sagefs hygiene --rescue <name>` puts a worktree's work on a branch. A checkout a cohort holds reads as in use, and a `*.tiers` directory beside the repository that nothing uses is listed as needing a look. A worktree outside the managed directory is asked about its work too and named when it holds some, and is never removed. There is no MCP tool for the rescue yet: it waits for the tool-list work. Code: [`SageFs/HygieneSweep.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs/HygieneSweep.fs)
- [x] **One command to set SageFs up in your agent.** The durable way to register SageFs is `claude mcp add sagefs -- sagefs mcp`, and the docs already say why an HTTP registration loses its tools when the daemon restarts: the session id lives in the daemon's memory and the client never asks for a new one. `sagefs setup` now prints, or with `--write` merges, the right snippet for Claude Code, VS Code, Cursor and Claude Desktop, keeps every other server in the file, leaves a file it cannot parse alone, refuses to overwrite a `sagefs` entry that points somewhere else, and installs the skill. The page is generated from the same code, and a test fails when it is stale. I read each client's own page for its file, key and entry shape on 2026-11-07, and the page names the source and the date next to each one. Cursor's table says `type: "stdio"` is required while its example leaves it out, so the snippet carries it. From nothing to a first eval takes two shell commands now, and still five tool calls against FsiMcp's one. What each client shows when the registered command is not on the path has not been read, and the seconds wait for the benchmark. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ClientSetup.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ClientSetup.fs)
- [x] **Help for one tool in sagefs call says what it takes.** `sagefs call send_fsharp_code --help` prints the tool's own sentence, one line for each parameter with its type and whether it is required (the same words a wrong call is refused with, read from the input schema the daemon sends), and where the full manual is: `discover_features` with `tool`, and `docs/mcp-tools.md`. `sagefs call --help` is still the command's usage. A name the daemon does not list is said so, with the nearest tool names and a pointer to `--list`. With no daemon running it prints the usage and how to start one, and exits 1. Code: [`SageFs.Core/McpCall.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/McpCall.fs)
- [x] **The daemon starts at login on macOS.** A launchd user agent starts the daemon at login and restarts its supervisor after a crash, the same job the systemd unit does on Linux. The README install fills in your home directory and your .NET folder, because launchd expands no variables. tw0po1nt wrote it and tested it on macOS 27 on an Apple Silicon Mac. An Intel Mac and the Homebrew dotnet formula are untested. Code: [`contrib/launchd/io.github.willehrendreich.sagefs.plist`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/contrib/launchd/io.github.willehrendreich.sagefs.plist)
- [x] **Builds SageFs starts no longer die on a leftover MSBuild node.** Session rebuilds and install-local's pack died with MSB4223 three times in one session under load, and they only proceeded once an agent exported MSBUILDDISABLENODEREUSE=1 by hand. The daemon's session rebuilds and its FSI host build now take the variable from one named list, and ship.fsx and install-local.fsx set it for every build they start. The skill's troubleshooting page names the error and the one-line fix for an older daemon. Code: [`SageFs.Core/ProcessEnvironment.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/ProcessEnvironment.fs)
- [x] **An interrupted gate cannot fail the run after it.** The gate reuses one checkout directory, and a killed run's versioned outputs crashed the next run in zero seconds with a FileNotFoundException naming a SageFs.Core version the tree no longer was. The gate now writes what it is doing beside the checkout before the pipeline starts and what it left once the pipeline ends on its own. A run that finds the first and no second clears the checkout's build output before it builds, and a checkout with no record is cleared too. A run that finished, even a red one, keeps its warm build. Code: [`SageFs.Core/GateCheckout.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/SageFs.Core/GateCheckout.fs)
- [x] **A failed gate's retry is one command.** A failed gate used to leave its bump commit behind, and a rerun added a second one that the pre-push hook refused only after a whole new gate. Now a plain `ship.fsx` looks at the release commits in origin/master..HEAD first. With none it bumps. With one that is above the published version it keeps that bump and gates HEAD. With two or more it stops before any gate, names the commits and prints the `git rebase --onto` line that drops each extra one. The hook counts release commits with the same reader, and the marker text lives in one place. The retry path is written up in docs/agents.md. Code: [`scripts/ReleaseRules.fs`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/scripts/ReleaseRules.fs)

### Docs and onboarding

- [x] **Published numbers for the REPL loop.** I timed an edit plus a check in a warm session against a build plus a filtered test on three projects, from 306 lines to 86,019. The check answered in 21 to 25 milliseconds on all three, because it does not care how big the project is, while the build took 2 to 52 seconds and cares a great deal. The table is in docs with the machine and the load averages it was measured under, and a snippet that cannot type-check returns its errors in 81 milliseconds, so the fast number is a real check rather than one that says fine. Code: [`docs/repl-loop-benchmarks.md`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/docs/repl-loop-benchmarks.md)
- [x] **What a new tool must declare is written down.** Adding list_members took six declarations, and it missed four hand-kept test lists as well, which left the default suite red on master. The tools page now lists all seven places in the order that keeps the build green, names the test that goes red for each, and says what else a tool commit carries: the Plugin trailer, and a name that is not a retired one. The slice plan in the progressive map research points there. Code: [`docs/mcp-tools.md`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/docs/mcp-tools.md)
- [x] **The Readme capability table says which rows are HTTP routes.** The ticks under MCP for completion and the type explorer were gone in March, but the cells that replaced them were a bare colon, which reads as a typo. The rows that are HTTP routes and no tool now say HTTP, every other empty cell says no, and the note under the table says what each word means. Code: [`Readme.md`](https://github.com/WillEhrendreich/SageFs/blob/master/Readme.md)
